# What this book is {.unnumbered}

This book is the guide to **ISLA** (Invariant Slice Attention), a neural
surrogate for steady, boundary-driven PDE problems: given a discretized
boundary and the problem's global conditions, predict the steady field on
that boundary and in the domain it bounds. It is written the way a user
guide for a design code is written. It teaches what the method computes and
why each part is there, shows how to run it, and then lays out, with the
same care, what the measurements say for it and against it. The reader we
have in mind is fluent in PDE numerics and machine learning and has never
seen this program; every term is defined where it first appears, and every
number is computed, as the page renders, from a checked-in artifact.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the name comes from"}
ISLA is pronounced "eye-la". An *isla* is an island: a shape defined
entirely by its boundary, which is what the method takes as input. The code
class is `ISLA` in `physicsnemo.experimental.nn`.
:::

## The thesis {#sec-verdict}

**ISLA matches GeoTransolver, the strongest published slice-attention
surrogate, in distribution at the recipe's default budget and adds a set of
exact guarantees that no other slice-attention model offers; where it still trails, the deficit is priced.** Four
things are true at once, and the book is organized around keeping all four
in view:

1. **In distribution, ISLA matches GeoTransolver and leads Transolver by 6%
   at the recipe's default budget; below full data it trails GeoTransolver
   by a deficit that narrows from 17% at 27 cars to zero at 435.** With every
   model given the same inputs and scored on the same instrument at the
   reporting protocol of 200,000 sampled cells per case, each at its own
   best learning rate, GeoTransolver and ISLA are at parity on DrivAerML
   (cars) at full data and Transolver trails both; on the smaller training
   sets GeoTransolver is the more data-efficient model, by a margin that
   closes monotonically with data (@sec-scoreboard-200k). On HiLiftAeroML
   (wings) the baselines lead by 21 to 32% on the small rungs, by 4 to 11% at
   210 random training cases, and by 2 to 5% where the validation geometries
   are never seen at 21 training geometries; the deficit is a small-data,
   recurring-geometry effect and does not move with the cell budget
   (@sec-data-efficiency).
2. **ISLA's guarantees are exact and they earn accuracy where they matter.**
   Rotation and translation covariance hold by construction, so when
   geometries arrive in arbitrary poses ISLA leads baselines that learned
   pose from augmentation. Its relative frame reads nothing from the sample,
   so its prediction is consistent under a change of surface sampling: when
   the inference draw on DrivAerML is biased 10:1 front to back at 100,000
   cells, ISLA's error grows by about 7% where GeoTransolver's grows about
   9x and Transolver's about 5x (@sec-consistency-bench), and its slices
   stay put when the draw changes (anchor motion 1/16 of GeoTransolver's,
   @sec-territories).
3. **Below 100,000 cells ISLA's error carries finite-sample noise in its
   slice integrals; at the protocol it is gone.** At 200,000 cells
   GeoTransolver and ISLA are at parity on DrivAerML (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA
   0.998); the gap smaller budgets showed at full data was count noise,
   which more cells remove (@sec-deficit-anatomy).
4. **ISLA learns the field, not the mesher's habits, and both architectures
   share one capacity floor.** Trained under an area-proportional sampling
   law instead of the uniform one and scored on the same uniform draw,
   GeoTransolver's error grows 2.6x on the wings and 7.9x on the cars,
   Transolver's 2.4x and 9.6x, and ISLA's 1% and 8%: a weak dependence,
   measured on two datasets (@sec-training-law). On DrivAerML at the
   100,000-cell scaling budget, ISLA's and GeoTransolver's capacity ladders
   end at the same floor of about 0.040, identical at matched parameters
   (about 140M), with ISLA within 1% of it at half GeoTransolver's
   parameters (@fig-capacity).

```{python}
#| label: setup-index
#| include: false
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
fp = lambda runs, keys, f="pressure_l2": [runs[k]["fields"][f]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]

# training-law study: each model trained under the uniform and under the area-proportional sampling law,
# scored on the independent uniform draw (wings: 35 HiLiftAeroML cases at 200,000 cells; cars: 435 DrivAerML cars at 100,000 cells)
TA = J("trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["arms"]; TAD = J("trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["arms"]
MODELS = (("isla", "isla_ref"), ("gt_unit", "gt"), ("transolver_unit", "t"))
law = {ds: {m: A[f"{m}_area"]["mean"]["unif"] / A[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["unif"] for m, _ in MODELS} for ds, A in (("wings", TA), ("cars", TAD))}
# sampling consistency at 100,000 cells: the uniform-trained arm scored on the 10:1 front/back biased draw ÷ on the uniform draw (cars)
dens = {m: TAD[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["biased"] / TAD[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["unif"] for m, _ in MODELS}
# interior: boundary -> volume at 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000 queries; linear ISLA at 5e-4 against GeoTransolver-volume
RV = J("ratevol_reduction_2026-09-20.json")
inter = RV["ratios_gt_vol_over_isla"]["isla_lr5e4"]
inter_isla = {f: RV["arms"]["isla_lr5e4"][f]["mean"] for f in ("pressure_l2", "velocity_l2", "nut_l2")}
inter_gt = {f: RV["arms"]["gt_vol_unit"][f]["mean"] for f in ("pressure_l2", "velocity_l2", "nut_l2")}
# capacity: the best lane of each architecture's ladder at 100,000 cells (cosine routing for ISLA's depth axis)
RN = J("routenorm_extension_2026-09-21.json")["configurations"]; CAPC = J("cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
cap = {"isla24": RN["isla|cos|w384|d24|lr5e-4"], "isla48": RN["isla|cos|w384|d48|lr2.5e-4"],
       "gt1024": CAPC["gt|w1024|d12|s256|lr1e3"], "gt2048": RN["gt|w2048|d12|lr1e-3"]}
M = lambda c: f"{c['params'] / 1e6:.0f}M"
# the reporting protocol: 200,000 cells per case, each architecture at its better learning rate
P2 = J("p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json")["arms"]
isla200 = P2["isla"]["pressure_mean"]; t200 = P2["transolver_unit_lr3e3"]["pressure_mean"]
_gts = {k: P2[k]["pressure_mean"] for k in ("gt_unit_lr1e3", "gt_unit_lr3e3") if P2[k]["pressure_mean"]}
gt200_key = min(_gts, key=_gts.get); gt200 = _gts[gt200_key]; gt200_lab = "3e-3" if gt200_key.endswith("3e3") else "1e-3"
PP = J("p200k_pose_reduction_2026-09-19.json")
pose200 = {"isla": PP["arms"]["isla"]["posed_over_native"], "gt": PP["arms"]["gt_unit"]["posed_over_native"], "t": PP["arms"]["transolver_unit"]["posed_over_native"]}
pose200_lead = {"gt": PP["verdict"]["gt_aug_posed_over_isla_posed"], "t": PP["verdict"]["t_aug_posed_over_isla_posed"]}
PL = J("p200k_ladder_interim_2026-09-18.json")["rungs"]
lad200 = {n: PL[f"n{n}"]["gt_over_isla_at_better_rates"] for n in (27, 54, 109, 218)}
```

rungs are in @sec-data-efficiency.

## The trade in one picture

**At full data on DrivAerML, ISLA gives up no in-distribution accuracy, and
when the sampling or the pose departs from the training conditions its
error barely moves where the baselines' grows several-fold.** @fig-headline
puts the two halves of the trade on one x-axis.

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The priced trade, on DrivAerML (435 training cars, 48 validation cars,
#|   float32). Top: in-distribution surface-pressure error at the reporting
#|   protocol of 200,000 cells per case, each architecture at its own best
#|   learning rate (GeoTransolver at 3e-3); lower is better, and ISLA and
#|   GeoTransolver are at parity. Bottom: how much each model's error grows
#|   when the evaluation or the training departs from the uniform-draw,
#|   native-pose convention, as a factor on a log axis where 1 means
#|   unaffected. Filled bars: the surface is sampled with a 10:1
#|   front-to-back density bias and each model's input frame is taken from
#|   the biased sample, at 100,000 cells (the scaling budget). Hatched bars:
#|   every training and validation case is placed in its own random pose, at
#|   200,000 cells; the baselines were trained with rotation augmentation,
#|   ISLA without. Dotted bars: the model is trained under the
#|   area-proportional sampling law instead of the uniform one and scored on
#|   the same uniform draw as its uniform-trained twin, at 100,000 cells.
#|   Colors and marks follow the book's key (@fig-key). How to read this:
#|   the top panel is the accuracy ISLA gives up, which at full data is
#|   none; the bottom panel is what its contracts buy. It does not show the
#|   HiLiftAeroML rungs, where the baselines lead on accuracy and where the
#|   training-law factors are 2.6x for GeoTransolver, 2.4x for Transolver
#|   and 0.99x for ISLA (35 wings, 200,000 cells), the smaller DrivAerML
#|   training sets, where GeoTransolver leads, or the interior task
#|   (@tbl-thesis). Data: as @tbl-thesis.
#| code-fold: true
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 6.2), sharex=True,
                               gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 1.15], hspace=0.12))
keys = ["isla_ref", "gt", "t"]
names = ["ISLA", "GeoTransolver", "Transolver"]
xs = np.arange(len(keys))
err = [isla200, gt200, t200]
for x, k, e in zip(xs, keys, err):
    ax0.bar(x, e, width=0.6, **bar_kwargs(k))
    ax0.text(x, e + 0.001, f"{e:.4f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax0.set_ylim(0, 0.07); ax0.set_yticks([0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06])
ax0.set_ylabel("surface pressure error,\narea-weighted relative L2 [–]")
ax0.set_title("in distribution at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells): lower is better")
ax0.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

dvals = [dens["isla"], dens["gt_unit"], dens["transolver_unit"]]
pvals = [pose200["isla"], pose200["gt"], pose200["t"]]
lvals = [law["cars"]["isla"], law["cars"]["gt_unit"], law["cars"]["transolver_unit"]]
w = 0.24
for x, k, d, p, l in zip(xs, keys, dvals, pvals, lvals):
    ax1.bar(x - w, d, width=w, **bar_kwargs(k))
    ax1.text(x - w, d * 1.12, f"{d:.2f}x", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
    ax1.bar(x, p, width=w, color=STYLE[k]["color"], hatch="///", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
    ax1.text(x, p * 1.12, f"{p:.2f}x", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
    ax1.bar(x + w, l, width=w, color=STYLE[k]["color"], hatch="..", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
    ax1.text(x + w, l * 1.12, f"{l:.2f}x", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
ax1.axhline(1.0, color=INK2, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
ax1.set_yscale("log"); ax1.set_ylim(0.8, 30)
ax1.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20]); ax1.set_yticklabels(["1", "2", "5", "10", "20"])
ax1.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
ax1.set_ylabel("error growth when conditions change,\nshifted ÷ in-distribution [–]")
ax1.set_title("out of the training conventions: 1 means unaffected")
ax1.set_xticks(xs); ax1.set_xticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
ax1.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax1.text(2.55, 1.0, " 1 = unaffected", va="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
ax1.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor=MUTED, label="inference draw with a 10:1 sampling-density bias, sample frame (100,000 cells)"),
                    Patch(facecolor=MUTED, hatch="///", edgecolor="white", label="every case in a random pose (200,000 cells)"),
                    Patch(facecolor=MUTED, hatch="..", edgecolor="white", label="trained under the area-proportional law ÷ trained uniform, scored on the uniform draw (100,000 cells)")],
           loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

## Names, symbols and colors {#sec-key}

**Every thing in this book has one name and every architecture one color,
and a ratio between architectures is always baseline ÷ ISLA.** The names
below are canonical; their definitions are in the chapters cited.

| Name | What it is | Where defined |
|---|---|---|
| **ISLA** | the model as shipped, named without qualifier: relative frame, RMS-pairwise-distance length unit, the class defaults | @sec-isla |
| **removed variants** (legacy centered, similarity gauge) | centered frames the class no longer has; they appear only in collapsed diagnostic notes, labeled | @sec-isla-variants |
| **ablation**, **diagnostic** | a configuration measured only to price a design choice (weights-off, raw coordinates); never adopted | @sec-principled-decisions |
| **GeoTransolver**, **Transolver**, **GeoTransolver-volume** | the public slice-attention baselines, named without qualifier and never modified. "GeoTransolver + ISLA's *feature* (ablation)" is a baseline with one of ISLA's features added to isolate an effect; it is not a variant of the public model | @sec-baselines |
| **unit-direction protocol** | every model receives the freestream as a unit vector; the fair-comparison rule that decides the surface ranking | @sec-fair-comparison |
| **global vector / scalar inputs** | the problem's global conditions ($K$ directions, $S$ scalars); here $K = 1$, the freestream direction, and $S = 0$ | @sec-isla-inputs |
| **measure weight** $w_i$ | the surface area a sampled cell stands for; the quadrature weight of every sum in the model | @sec-isla-quadrature |
| **relative frame** | ISLA's construction of position: no center, positions used only as differences to anchors, the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample as length unit | @sec-isla-frame |
| **slice**, **anchor** | a soft group of tokens, and its measure-weighted mean position and normal | @sec-isla-slices |
| **relational invariants** | the scalars that describe a token relative to an anchor | @sec-isla-relational |
| **area-weighted relative L2**, **float32 instrument** | the metric and the precision every reported number is scored at | @sec-metrics |
| **rung** | one training-set size on the data-efficiency ladder ("the 35-case rung") | @sec-data-efficiency |
| **deficit anatomy** | the decomposition of the in-distribution gap into measured parts | @sec-deficit-anatomy |
| **form** | a structural choice of the architecture (one routing per layer, the head basis) as opposed to its capacity or its inputs | @sec-deficit-anatomy |

```{python}
#| label: fig-key
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The book's visual key. Each architecture keeps its hue in every figure;
#|   a variant of an architecture is the same hue at a lighter tint with an
#|   open marker, and an ablation is hatched. Color is never the only cue:
#|   the marker shape and the line style carry the same distinction. ISLA's
#|   two removed frame variants (legacy centered, similarity gauge) share the
#|   light blue with open markers and appear only inside collapsed diagnostic
#|   notes.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 1.9))
order = ["isla_ref", "isla_abl", "gt", "gt_var", "t", "t_var"]  # the two frame variants live only in diagnostic notes
for i, k in enumerate(order):
    y = -(i % 3); col = i // 3
    x0 = 0.05 + col * 0.5
    kw = series_kwargs(k, lw=2.0, ms=8)
    ax.plot([x0, x0 + 0.08], [y, y], **{a: kw[a] for a in ("color", "ls", "lw")})
    ax.plot([x0 + 0.04], [y], marker=kw["marker"], ms=8, mfc=kw["mfc"], mec=kw["mec"], mew=1.8, ls="none", color=kw["color"])
    if STYLE[k]["hatch"]:
        ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Rectangle((x0 + 0.10, y - 0.3), 0.04, 0.6, **bar_kwargs(k)))
    ax.text(x0 + 0.16, y, STYLE[k]["label"], va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 0.6)
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_aspect("auto")
plt.show()
```

Two conventions hold in every table and figure. **A ratio between
architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error**, so a value above
one favors ISLA. **Every error is the area-weighted relative L2 of
@sec-metrics, scored in float32** on the final-epoch checkpoint. A few
within-grid comparisons (learning-rate grids, resource controls) were scored
in bfloat16 and are labeled as such in their captions; no bfloat16 number
is compared across architectures.

## How to read this book {#sec-how-to-read}

**The book is in five parts and reads in order; each part assumes only the
ones before it.**

- **Part I, the problem** (@sec-problem). What a boundary-to-field surrogate
  is, taught on a two-dimensional airfoil whose exact solution we know; the
  two production datasets and their splits; the metric; the frozen protocol.
- **Part II, the architecture.** @sec-isla builds ISLA one idea at a time,
  from "a sum over cells should be an integral" to the equivariant output
  basis, with a figure for each idea and the derivations folded away.
  @sec-architecture then states the forward pass exactly, stage by stage,
  with every tensor shape and code identifier. @sec-baselines
  describes GeoTransolver and Transolver and the fair-comparison rules.
- **Part III, using ISLA** (@sec-using). The one configuration and its
  options, the inputs the model accepts, the recipe commands, the
  learning-rate rule for linear routing and the bounded-routing alternative,
  the inference sampler, checkpoints and cost.
- **Part IV, evidence.** @sec-scoreboard is the standing on one page. Behind
  it: data efficiency on the wings (@sec-data-efficiency); accuracy at full
  data, robustness and the deficit anatomy (@sec-full-data); interior
  prediction (@sec-interior).
- **Part V, limits and status.** @sec-limits states the limit of each claim
  and what would move it. @sec-program-status is the live research tech tree.
- **Appendices.** The design-decision ledger (@sec-principled-decisions), and
  the dated lab notebook (@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and
  verdict, including the failures, in the order they happened.

Optional depth sits in collapsed notes like the one at the top of this
page. The throughline reads completely with all of them closed.

## What this book does not claim {#sec-not-claimed}

**Each claim in this book has a scope, and the list below names what sits
outside it.**

- **Not that ISLA is more accurate in distribution.** At the reporting
  protocol ISLA and GeoTransolver are at parity on DrivAerML at full data
  (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.998); GeoTransolver leads by up to 17% below full
  data on the cars and by 27% on the 35-wing rung (@sec-scoreboard-200k).
  Comparisons against baselines fed the physical freestream velocity measure
  the protocol's input scale, not the architectures, and appear only as such
  (@sec-part-baseline).
- **Not that equivariance is an accuracy edge on posed data in general.** A
  baseline trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at about a
  percent of cost (@sec-pose). ISLA's pose lead is against baselines that learn
  pose from augmentation, in random poses.
- **Not that sampling consistency is an invariance.** It is a fine-mesh-limit
  property: ISLA's small degradation under a 10:1 bias is 1.07x at 100,000
  cells on DrivAerML, a single dataset for this probe (@sec-consistency-bench).
- **Not that ISLA is indifferent to the training sampling law.** Trained
  under the area-proportional law and scored on the uniform draw, its error
  moves 1% on the wings and 8% on the cars; why the cars show the larger
  dependence is open (@sec-training-law).
- **Not that cosine routing buys accuracy.** It is the default (2026-09-22)
  because it removes the learning-rate ceiling on both datasets; accuracy is
  neutral to linear routing on the cars and 6% better on the 35-wing rung,
  and the evidence lanes trained before the change use linear routing
  (@sec-using-lr).
- **Not that the interior lead is unconditional.** It is on velocity only, and
  the interacting decode requires at least the training count of points to be
  queried together (@sec-interior-companion).
- **Not that either architecture extrapolates across a flow regime** or
  transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle family (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Not that the HiLift figures are test-set figures.** They are validation
  figures on final-epoch checkpoints; the sealed test was spent on regime
  extrapolation (@sec-limits-validation).
